figures.title: Historical commercial KPI dashboard
figures.interpretation: These KPIs use explicit transaction populations. Sales before credits are not accounting net revenue, and the 65.58% repeat share is a within-window description of identified purchasers rather than a cohort-retention estimate.
figures.observation: £10,642,110.80 sales before credits; £893,979.73 credits; £9,748,131.07 credit-adjusted value.
figures.business_implication: Agree the financial measurement basis before comparing performance or assigning targets.

figures.title: Sales, credits and other adjustments
figures.interpretation: Three valid transaction-value bases coexist. The all-line signed amount is £9,726,006.95, not the before-credit sales figure. The bridge explains the numerical difference instead of choosing an ambiguous “net revenue” label.
figures.observation: £10,642,110.80 before credits becomes £9,748,131.07 after £893,979.73 in C-credit notes; the remaining financial adjustments total −£22,124.12.
figures.business_implication: Use a reconciled finance/BI definition and retain an adjustment register before setting or comparing sales targets.

figures.title: Monthly demand with partial-month warning
figures.interpretation: Gross and credit-adjusted series share a clear autumn increase, but the last data point is not a comparable full month. November growth of 30.63% is volume-led because invoice count rises faster than total sales.
figures.observation: November 2011 reaches £1,503,866.78 on 2,769 invoices; October is £1,151,263.73 on 2,040 invoices. December 2011 covers only 1–9 December.
figures.business_implication: Validate the pattern on fresh multi-year data, then test capacity and availability plans rather than extrapolating a nine-day month.

figures.title: Credit frequency and value severity are different
figures.interpretation: Counts alone rank exposure differently from value-weighted severity. Monthly credits may relate to sales from earlier periods; credit value divided by same-month sales is a period activity ratio, not a cohort return rate. The large January and December offset pairs and partial-month coverage also matter.
figures.observation: November has the most C-credit documents (441) but credit value is 3.17% of its sales. January’s ratio is 19.04%; partial December’s is 32.16%.
figures.business_implication: Monitor both credit-document share and credit value/sales, with reason codes and links to original invoices before interpreting a process failure.

figures.title: Customer concentration on the identified-sales basis
figures.interpretation: Value is concentrated, but the observed threshold is not an exact 80/20 rule. Anonymous sales (£1,754,901.91) sit outside this customer curve, so concentration cannot be asserted for every real purchaser.
figures.observation: 1,130 customers (26.05% of 4,338) reach 80% of £8,887,208.89 identified sales. The top 43 IDs contribute 31.84% of that pool.
figures.business_implication: Validate current major accounts and credit quality; maintain service coverage without assuming a rank is a lifetime-value estimate.

figures.title: RFM segment size versus value contribution
figures.interpretation: Segment headcount and commercial value differ substantially. The segment shares use identified before-credit sales; Champions’ share of all qualified sales is 53.84%. RFM labels are heuristic and tie-dependent.
figures.observation: Champions number 942 (21.72% of identified purchasers) and supply 64.47% of known sales. At Risk plus Can’t Lose Them contains 658 IDs.
figures.business_implication: Refresh contact eligibility, credit-adjusted balances and segment rules before retention or win-back tests. Do not call all historic segment value recoverable.

figures.title: Product leaders before and after recorded credits
figures.interpretation: A gross-only catalogue ranking can overstate recorded credit-adjusted transaction value. Two conspicuous bulk transactions are fully offset, but the records remain valid observations in their respective sales/credit views.
figures.observation: 23843 falls from £168,469.60 to £0.00; 23166 falls from £81,700.92 to £4,221.28. 22423 has £164,459.49 after recorded credits.
figures.business_implication: Use credit-aware SKU measures plus stock, margin and lead-time data before changing replenishment or promotions.

figures.title: Leading non-UK countries
figures.interpretation: The bar chart isolates export comparisons that would otherwise be compressed by UK dominance. Netherlands’ large value does not imply broad customer depth: its top account is 98.16% of identified country sales.
figures.observation: Netherlands leads at £285,446.34, followed by EIRE £283,140.52, Germany £228,678.40 and France £209,625.37. UK sales are £9,001,744.09.
figures.business_implication: Separate key-account protection from geographic acquisition. Compare customer breadth and delivered margin before proposing expansion.

figures.title: Invoice-value histogram: mean versus typical order
figures.interpretation: The log x-axis preserves all positive invoices and makes the severe right tail visible. Equal-width log bins are counts in multiplicative intervals, not a linear-scale density. Mean and median represent different aspects of this distribution.
figures.observation: The complete 19,960-invoice distribution has mean £533.17, median £303.30, 99th percentile £4,821.17 and maximum £168,469.60.
figures.business_implication: Report a median, IQR and tail percentiles alongside AOV; do not design standard service or demand assumptions around mean alone.

figures.title: Basket breadth versus invoice value
figures.interpretation: Wider baskets tend to have larger values, with substantial dispersion and extreme observations on logarithmic axes. Line count is not necessarily distinct SKU count and is not an exogenous driver.
figures.observation: Across all qualified invoices, Spearman correlation between sales-line count and invoice value is 0.551606. Each plotted point represents one invoice; no point is sampled away.
figures.business_implication: Treat basket-building as a hypothesis for a controlled test; do not translate correlation into a promised cross-sell percentage.

figures.title: Annotated Spearman correlation heatmap
figures.interpretation: Quantity is more strongly rank-associated with recorded value than unweighted line mean price. These variables mechanically contribute to value and may reflect wholesale mix. Cyclic month/hour integers and customer IDs are excluded from the numerical heatmap.
figures.observation: Value correlates 0.838984 with total quantity, 0.551606 with sales-line count and 0.094257 with unweighted mean unit amount.
figures.business_implication: Investigate quantity/basket mix and unit economics using proper margin and experimental evidence; the heatmap is not a price-optimisation model.

figures.title: Weekday sales and first-recorded invoice hour
figures.interpretation: Mutually exclusive earliest-timestamp allocation fixes double counting from invoices that span two line-recording minutes. The aggregate time profile is a billing-data description, not proof of opening hours, labour load or fulfilment times.
figures.observation: Thursday contributes £2,199,292.57; noon starts 3,219 qualified invoices. There are no Saturday records in the workbook.
figures.business_implication: Compare fresh operational timestamps, order processing effort and service levels before scheduling staff or systems capacity.

figures.title: Box plot of UK and non-UK invoice values
figures.interpretation: Both groups have substantial high-value tails. Whiskers use 1.5×IQR on the original data, then the y-axis is displayed logarithmically. Outlier points remain. Invoice comparisons are descriptive because repeat customers contribute multiple observations.
figures.observation: UK median invoice value is £299.95 (Q1 £147.06; Q3 £465.315) versus non-UK £424.06 (Q1 £228.84; Q3 £790.54). Group sizes are 18,019 and 1,941 invoices.
figures.business_implication: Prefer the customer-level comparison for conditional inference and evaluate delivery/margin constraints before treating larger foreign invoices as attractive acquisition economics.

figures.title: Count plot of observed customer purchase frequency
figures.interpretation: Each identified purchaser appears exactly once, so the bars sum to 4,338. The observed repeat majority does not remove acquisition-date censoring or missing-customer bias. A count plot is used instead of an unnecessary pie chart.
figures.observation: Frequency bands contain 1,493 customers with one invoice; 835 with two; 1,138 with 3–5; 535 with 6–10; and 337 with at least 11.
figures.business_implication: Build exposure-adjusted cohorts from current customer data and measure repeat activity over a common follow-up window.

figures.title: Qualified line quantity and unit-amount distributions
figures.interpretation: The two positive measures have very different units and long tails. Separate panels and logarithmic x-axes preserve every qualified line without implying quantity and currency are directly comparable. The unit-amount panel includes all qualified codes, including non-product entries.
figures.observation: Quantity median is 4, mean 10.616600 and maximum 80,995. Unit amount median is £2.08, mode £1.25 and qualified maximum £13,541.33.
figures.business_implication: Use a merchandise-only, credit-aware demand layer for replenishment and retain an exception review for unusually large amounts rather than applying a universal cutoff.

worked_examples.title: one recorded line value
worked_examples.formula: L = Q × P, where Q is recorded quantity and P is the unit amount in GBP.
worked_examples.result: The recorded positive line value is £15.30.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is a before-credit transaction amount, not margin or proof of cash collection. The product name is WHITE HANGING HEART T-LIGHT HOLDER.

worked_examples.title: complete invoice aggregation
worked_examples.formula: sum quantity × price across seven lines

worked_examples.title: missingness and duplicate proportions
worked_examples.formula: Missing % = missing rows / all source rows × 100; duplicate % = exact duplicate rows / all source rows × 100.
worked_examples.result: About one quarter of raw lines cannot be assigned to a known customer; fewer than 1% are exact duplicate entries.
worked_examples.interpretation: The denominators are raw rows, not customer counts. The two flags may overlap; their percentages should not be added as a total error rate.

worked_examples.title: sample mean, variance and standard deviation
worked_examples.formula: sum squared deviations / (n−1), then square root
worked_examples.interpretation: Arithmetic illustration only, not a random sample.

worked_examples.title: global AOV and the actual median positions
worked_examples.formula: AOV = Σ sales invoice values / number of sales invoices. For even n, median = (value at position n/2 + value at position n/2 + 1)/2 in ascending order.
worked_examples.result: Reported AOV £533.17; median £303.30. Mean/median − 1 = 0.757902684, or approximately 75.79%.
worked_examples.interpretation: The mean is not the typical invoice. Both central tendency and tail quantiles should be reported; the gap is descriptive evidence of right skew, not proof of invalid records.

worked_examples.title: IQR fences and a retained real observation
worked_examples.formula: IQR = Q3 − Q1; lower fence = Q1 − 1.5×IQR; upper fence = Q3 + 1.5×IQR.
worked_examples.substitution: Qualified Quantity: Q1 = 1, Q3 = 11; IQR = 10. Lower = 1 − 15 = −14; upper = 11 + 15 = 26. Invoice 536367 / StockCode 84879 has Quantity 32, so 32 > 26. Its value is 32 × £1.69 = £54.08.
worked_examples.result: 27,111 of 524,878 sales lines are flagged: 27,111 / 524,878 × 100 = 5.165200%, reported as 5.17%. All remain in the sales dataset.
worked_examples.interpretation: A generic IQR rule identifies unusual quantities, not confirmed errors. Deleting this legitimate-looking line merely for exceeding 26 would erase actual recorded demand.

worked_examples.title: UK sales-value share
worked_examples.formula: Country sales share = country qualified sales / all qualified sales × 100.
worked_examples.result: 84.59% of qualified sales value is assigned to the United Kingdom.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is value-weighted share after deduplication, not the 91.43% UK share of raw lines and not a national market-share estimate. Domestic demand dominates this retailer’s recorded sales.

worked_examples.title: November growth decomposed into invoices and AOV
worked_examples.formula: Growth % = (current − prior)/prior × 100. Sales ratio = invoice-count ratio × AOV ratio.
worked_examples.result: Sales grew 30.63%; more invoices outweighed a 3.76% lower average invoice value.
worked_examples.interpretation: The peak is invoice-volume-led, not evidence of a price increase. AOV is a mix of prices, quantities, products and customers; it cannot isolate price behaviour. Both months are fully observed.

worked_examples.title: credit denominators and the financial bridge
worked_examples.formula: Adjusted value = sales before credits − absolute recorded C-credit value. Credit-document share = C-credit IDs / (sales IDs + C-credit IDs).
worked_examples.result: Credit-adjusted value £9,748,131.07; all-line signed value £9,726,006.95; document share 16.12%; credit-value ratio 8.40%.
worked_examples.interpretation: The 16.12% counts documents while 8.40% measures value. Neither is a linked-order cancellation probability. Using all 25,900 raw IDs instead gives 14.81%; using credits/(sales + absolute credits) gives the legacy 7.75% activity share. Different denominators cannot be used interchangeably.

worked_examples.title: repeat share and segment-denominator discipline
worked_examples.formula: Repeat share = purchasers with >1 qualified invoice / identified purchasers. Segment value share requires a stated sales denominator.
worked_examples.result: 65.58% observed repeat share; Champions contribute 64.47% of identified sales, equivalent to 53.84% of all sales.
worked_examples.interpretation: The larger segment-value share is not the segment’s share of all revenue. Missing IDs remain outside RFM, and the repeat statistic is not cohort-adjusted retention.

worked_examples.title: manual Pearson correlation
worked_examples.interpretation: Five-invoice arithmetic only; full-data rank association differs.

worked_examples.title: manual customer-level Welch test
worked_examples.formula: Welch standard error, t and Satterthwaite degrees of freedom
worked_examples.interpretation: Conditional exploratory group comparison, not causation.

worked_examples.title: chi-square and repeat status
worked_examples.interpretation: No detected association, not evidence of equivalence.

worked_examples.title: outlier and deduplication sensitivity, not a replacement result
worked_examples.formula: Sensitivity change % = (alternative total − published sales total)/published sales total × 100.
worked_examples.substitution: Capping each qualified line at its actual 99th percentile of £183.60 gives £8,907,983.82. (£8,907,983.82 − £10,642,110.804)/£10,642,110.804 × 100 = −16.294953%, reported as −16.29%. Keeping all exact duplicates instead gives £10,666,684.54, £24,573.74 above the published deduplicated basis.
worked_examples.result: A generic cap materially lowers recorded activity; exact-duplicate treatment has a much smaller 0.23% effect relative to the no-dedup basis.
worked_examples.interpretation: These are transparent alternative definitions, not verified correction amounts, forecasts or realised business benefits. Retaining valid extreme records and checking credits is more defensible than silently clipping them.

findings.title: Sales activity is not retained or accounting revenue
findings.evidence: Sales before credits are £10,642,110.80; C-credit notes are £893,979.73.
findings.comparison: The resulting £9,748,131.07 differs again from the £9,726,006.95 all-line signed amount after bad-debt adjustments.
findings.meaning: The measurement basis changes the answer, not merely its wording.
findings.importance: Ambiguous net-revenue labels would obscure credit exposure and inconsistent targets.
findings.recommendation: Publish the three separately defined measures and a signed adjustment bridge.

findings.title: Two fully offset bulk entries dominate credit severity
findings.evidence: The 581483/C581484 and 541431/C541433 pairs total £245,653.20 gross and zero signed pair value.
findings.comparison: They alone account for 27.48% of recorded C-credit value; 23843 goes from £168,469.60 to £0.00.
findings.meaning: A small number of extreme records can alter product rankings and period credit ratios.
findings.importance: Treating these gross values as replenishment demand or loyal-customer value would misallocate attention.
findings.recommendation: Prioritise traceable credit linkage and inspect large offsets without deleting authentic records or alleging a cause.

findings.title: AOV is materially above the typical invoice
findings.evidence: Mean invoice value is £533.17 versus median £303.30, with p99 £4,821.17.
findings.comparison: A hypothetical £183.60 line-value cap lowers total sales by 16.29%, much more than the 0.23% deduplication sensitivity.
findings.meaning: The upper tail matters financially but does not justify arbitrary clipping.
findings.importance: A mean-only view masks both normal-sized orders and exceptional exposure.
findings.recommendation: Use median/IQR/tail percentiles alongside AOV and retain credit-qualified extreme observations.

findings.title: Identity coverage is a value-attribution limitation, not a reason to erase sales
findings.comparison: They supply 16.49% of all sales; known purchasers cover £8,887,208.89 (83.51%).
findings.meaning: Line missingness and financial coverage differ; a quarter of lines missing an ID does not mean a quarter of sales value is missing.
findings.importance: RFM and repeat findings cannot represent the complete purchaser population, and missingness may be selective.
findings.recommendation: Retain anonymous transactions in finance/time views and improve permissioned prospective identity linkage.

findings.title: Repeat activity does not imply a larger mean order
findings.comparison: Mean customer AOV is £421.00 for repeat versus £411.25 for one-time purchasers (Welch p 0.8732), while medians are £302.56 and £255.91 and the rank test differs.
findings.meaning: Mean, median and distributional questions produce different evidence; non-significance is not equivalence.
findings.importance: Retention economics may depend on frequency and credit-qualified contribution, not automatically higher mean AOV.
findings.recommendation: Test retention effects using current cohorts, common follow-up and appropriate contribution metrics.

findings.title: Customer concentration is strong but denominator-sensitive
findings.comparison: This is 64.47% of identified sales but only 53.84% of all sales; 1,130 IDs, not exactly 20%, reach 80% of the identified pool.
findings.meaning: The retailer has concentrated known-account value, not a universal 80/20 law.
findings.importance: Ignoring anonymous sales or credit balances overstates the reach and certainty of a CRM list.
findings.recommendation: Refresh key accounts, display both denominators and validate current credit-adjusted eligibility.

findings.title: A high gross customer ranking can disappear after credits
findings.evidence: Customer 16446 has £168,472.50 gross sales but £2.90 credit-adjusted; customer 12346 has £77,183.60 gross and £0.00 adjusted.
findings.comparison: Twenty-one purchasers have a non-positive penny-rounded adjusted balance in the observation window.
findings.meaning: Gross-only RFM can label large reversed transactions as customer value.
findings.importance: This risks inappropriate incentives, but the balances do not identify lifetime loss or misconduct.
findings.recommendation: Supplement rather than silently overwrite gross RFM with transparent credit-adjusted review flags.

findings.title: Win-back scope is historical exposure, not recoverable revenue
findings.evidence: At Risk plus Can’t Lose Them includes 658 purchasers and £818,896.54 of historical gross value.
findings.comparison: Recorded customer credits reduce that to £736,853.23; one member has a non-positive adjusted balance.
findings.meaning: A segment total describes what was recorded, not what an outreach campaign can recapture.
findings.importance: Presenting it as forecast recovery would invent conversion, permission and uplift assumptions.
findings.recommendation: Validate fresh permissions, exclude unresolved credit issues and measure a holdout-based campaign before scaling.

findings.title: Country value can represent one account rather than market breadth
findings.evidence: The UK generates £9,001,744.09 (84.59% of sales); Netherlands leads non-UK at £285,446.34.
findings.comparison: The leading Netherlands account supplies 98.16% of identified country sales across nine known IDs, while Germany has 94 and France 87 known purchasers.
findings.meaning: High national sales and broad demand are different dimensions.
findings.importance: Account loss could dominate the apparent national opportunity; acquisition economics remain unknown.
findings.recommendation: Protect current account relationships separately from small, cost-qualified market-expansion tests.

findings.title: The November peak is invoice-volume-led
findings.evidence: November sales of £1,503,866.78 exceed October by 30.63%.
findings.comparison: Invoice count rises 35.74% (2,040 to 2,769), while AOV falls 3.76% (£564.34 to £543.11).
findings.meaning: More invoices, not higher average invoice value, explain the growth identity.
findings.importance: A price-increase interpretation would misdirect peak planning; the nine-day December observation is also not comparable.
findings.recommendation: Validate current invoice workload, product availability and capacity before planning the next peak.

findings.title: Foreign customer AOV is higher, without a stronger repeat signal
findings.evidence: Mean customer AOV is £661.12 non-UK versus £391.68 UK; Welch p = 5.55×10⁻⁸, d = −0.150 for UK minus non-UK.
findings.comparison: Repeat shares are almost equal, 65.79% versus 65.56%, with Yates p = 0.9687.
findings.meaning: Higher invoice values and observed repeat share within the recorded window need not move together.
findings.importance: Country mix, costs, selection and tenure could explain patterns; neither comparison estimates a geography effect.
findings.recommendation: Compare delivered contribution and customer exposure before prioritising a country; test rather than infer causation.

findings.title: Basket associations suggest hypotheses, not demonstrated uplift
findings.evidence: Spearman value–quantity correlation is 0.838984 and value–line-count is 0.551606.
findings.comparison: Value–unweighted-mean-unit-amount correlation is only 0.094257; 825 of 3,912 merchandise codes reach 80% of merchandise gross sales.
findings.meaning: Basket mix and product concentration are operationally relevant, but value is mechanically constructed from quantity and price.
findings.importance: A heatmap cannot establish that increasing quantity or recommendations will improve profit.
findings.recommendation: Use credit-aware catalogue priorities and a pre-specified bundle/recommendation test with margin and credit guardrails.

recommendations.title: Reconcile finance definitions and implement credit traceability
recommendations.problem_evidence: £10.642m before-credit sales, £9.748m credit-adjusted value and £9.726m all-line signed value are different. Two offset pairs represent 27.48% of credit value.
recommendations.action: Create a versioned metric dictionary; retain all signed records; add an original-invoice link, reason code and exception queue to each new credit. Review large matched offsets before performance reporting.
recommendations.expected_benefit: Less misclassification of sales and more interpretable credit exposure; no financial saving is established by this dataset.
recommendations.measurement: Reconciliation residual should equal £0.00 at the documented rounding basis. Measure credit-link coverage, missing reason-code share and exception age; the source lacks the first two baselines, so establish them on new data rather than inventing them.

recommendations.title: Improve permissioned customer attribution without dropping anonymous activity
recommendations.problem_evidence: 132,186 qualified lines lack an ID; £1,754,901.91 (16.49% of sales) cannot be assigned to a known purchaser.
recommendations.action: Audit checkout and CRM linkage, preserve valid anonymous transactions and add optional, consent-compliant identifier capture with ID quality checks. Do not infer identity from purchase resemblance.
recommendations.expected_benefit: Broader, more representative CRM measurement while preserving full commercial totals and appropriate privacy choices.
recommendations.measurement: Track both known-sales value coverage (historical 83.51%) and missing-ID line share (25.18% in qualified sales). Report weekly changes with a fresh baseline and monitor abandoned checkout/consent complaints; do not set forced identity capture as the success condition.
recommendations.owner: CRM operations and data engineering with privacy review

recommendations.title: Protect validated high-value accounts before generic promotions
recommendations.problem_evidence: 942 Champions provide 64.47% of identified sales, but gross value can be misleading: customer 16446 has only £2.90 after recorded credits.
recommendations.action: Refresh the RFM window, permissions, account status and credit-adjusted balances; review high-concentration accounts with service teams. Keep gross and adjusted versions visible, and use a holdout where contact is discretionary.
recommendations.expected_benefit: More relevant service and less incentive spend on reversed activity. Improved retention is possible but not demonstrated.
recommendations.measurement: Measure current qualified repeat activity, credit-adjusted contribution per eligible account, service issues and opt-outs over a common follow-up period. Pre-specify treatment/control and decision criteria after costs and sample size are known; do not promise an uplift.

recommendations.title: Use a bounded, eligibility-checked win-back pilot
recommendations.problem_evidence: 658 At Risk/Can’t Lose Them IDs represent £736,853.23 of adjusted historical value, not recoverable sales; one has a non-positive adjusted balance.
recommendations.action: Revalidate current contact permission and trading status, resolve credits first and draw a small randomized eligible pilot with a business-as-usual holdout. Use recent recency/frequency definitions, not 2011 labels operationally.
recommendations.expected_benefit: Tests whether outreach adds incremental, retained value without presenting historical exposure as a forecast.
recommendations.measurement: Primary outcome: net-of-credit contribution per eligible assigned customer; secondary outcomes: repeat purchase, opt-outs and campaign cost. Set follow-up, minimum detectable effect and sample size from current data. Publish confidence intervals and costs before scaling.

recommendations.title: Prioritise credit-aware merchandise and integrate inventory economics
recommendations.problem_evidence: 23843 has £168,469.60 gross but £0.00 adjusted; 22423 has £164,459.49 after recorded credits. A set of 825 of 3,912 merchandise codes reaches 80% of gross merchandise value.
recommendations.action: Build a SKU scorecard with gross/credit-adjusted value, units, credit incidence, availability, margin and supplier lead time. Separate postage/manual codes. Investigate reversed bulk entries rather than treating them as ordinary replenishment demand.
recommendations.expected_benefit: Better prioritisation of stock reviews and less gross-ranking distortion; reduced stock-outs or cash tied in inventory cannot be quantified from these data.
recommendations.measurement: With inventory/cost data, monitor fill rate, stock-out days, contribution after credits and inventory turns by priority SKU. Compare against an agreed baseline and keep availability changes separate from demand changes.

recommendations.title: Plan peak workload from invoice volume, then validate operational effort
recommendations.problem_evidence: November invoice count increases 35.74% while AOV declines 3.76%; the modal recorded start hour is noon with 3,219 invoices across the extract.
recommendations.action: Refresh multiple years of demand and join warehouse/service timestamps. Stress-test invoice-processing and fulfilment capacity for observed order-count variation; separate billing times from physical workload.
recommendations.expected_benefit: A workload-led capacity plan is better aligned with the observed growth pattern than a price-led story, but no staffing saving or service improvement has been measured.
recommendations.measurement: Use current invoices/hour, processing minutes/order, backlog, on-time dispatch and error rate. Set service-level and capacity gates using current workload; explicitly compare complete months and avoid extrapolating the partial December record.
recommendations.owner: Operations manager with analytics and systems teams

recommendations.title: Separate key-account protection from geographic expansion
recommendations.problem_evidence: Netherlands leads non-UK value (£285,446.34) but one account supplies 98.16% of identified country sales; Germany/France show broader historical customer counts (94/87).
recommendations.action: Review current Netherlands and Australia key accounts separately from market-acquisition opportunities. For any expansion pilot, obtain shipping, tax, returns and landed-margin data and cap pilot exposure under approved budgets.
recommendations.expected_benefit: Makes concentration risk explicit and avoids mistaking one buyer’s demand for a broad national market.
recommendations.measurement: Track top-account share, active buyer breadth, delivered contribution, repeat activity, credit value and acquisition cost. Expansion passes a pre-agreed contribution/retention gate on current data, not simply a country gross-sales rank.
recommendations.owner: Commercial lead, account manager and finance

recommendations.title: Test basket-building rather than monetising correlation
recommendations.problem_evidence: Value–line-count Spearman 0.551606 and value–quantity 0.838984 suggest basket hypotheses, while repeat/one-time mean AOV differs little under Welch (p 0.8732).
recommendations.action: Develop plausible complementary-product suggestions using merchandise transactions, then randomize eligible customers or sessions if appropriate data become available. Pre-register the outcome, assignment unit, exclusions and credit follow-up.
recommendations.expected_benefit: Can distinguish incremental contribution from selection and larger-basket mechanics; no observed cross-sell lift or price elasticity is claimed.
recommendations.measurement: Measure contribution per assigned unit, conversion only if session denominators exist, credit-adjusted AOV, credit incidence and opt-outs. Compute a current-data power plan and report effect intervals. Stop or revise if margin/credit guardrails deteriorate.
